narrative_md:
## Audit summary (illustrative example)

Baseline for the full-floor suite: 138,091 kWh of electricity and 5,068 kWh of gas a year, about $12,611 (range $9,963 to $18,663). Office hot water is not modelled. The electricity price is a published Texas average, not your tariff, and gas is priced at the EIA Texas commercial average. The figures are simulated on the example weather year, not the site's own typical-year file, so they will move when that file is present. No bills were given, so the model is not calibrated to bills and every saving below is an uncalibrated estimate. The modelled gas use is low against surveyed offices of this size, and the benchmark asks for a check of the model before relying on it.

The plan follows a consultant's loading order: operations first, then load reduction, then equipment, and solar last, sized against the electricity that is left. Within each step the most cost-effective measure goes first, and a measure is recommended only if its savings-to-investment ratio (SIR) is at least 1. Within the $50,000 budget it selects, in that order, desk placement (no cost, saving about $68 a year) and LED lighting ($43,680, saving about $3,931 a year): $43,680 upfront, saving about $3,999 a year (range $2,673 to $5,949).

Solar comes last and is skipped as not cost-effective: Texas has no export price, so only the share the suite uses itself earns the retail price, and at the published Texas price an array costs more over its life than it saves.

Air sealing, rooftop unit replacement, lighting controls and window replacement cost more over their life than they save (SIR below 1), so they are neither recommended nor offered for financing. Nothing is financeable: the property is inside the City of Houston PACE region, but no measure left over is cost-effective, so there is nothing to put to a C-PACE programme.

A smart thermostat and an economizer save nothing in the model; plug-load management, window film and shades have no verified cost and need a quote. The suite sits under conditioned floors, so roof insulation and a cool roof do not apply to it.

Vexcel counts four rooftop units, so unit replacement and an economizer were evaluated: replacement is not cost-effective and the economizer saves nothing in the model. Aerial captures also disagree about the roof: four other captures outline a much larger structure than the tower that matches CoStar's floor plate, which the design uses.

Value uplift: capitalised at the rates of 16 comparable sales, the plan's savings correspond to about $22,218 of property value (range $0 to $84,980). This is an estimate shown beside the totals; it is not added to the savings.

Open question: the lighting power density. The analysis found that the answer could change the measures the plan picks; until it is given, the plan uses the most likely value.
